slides.heading: Quickselect
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Hard · Searching
slides.narration: Let's solve Quickselect, a hard searching problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Kth smallest element (1-based) of an unsorted array, in place with Hoare-style partitioning.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Kth smallest element (1-based) of an unsorted array, in place with Hoare-style partitioning.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Partition like quicksort, but only recurse into the side containing the kth position.
slides.narration: Partition like quicksort, but only recurse into the side containing the kth position.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Heap of size k → O(n log k)
slides.narration: Sorting finds the k-th smallest in n log n. A heap of size k is n log k. Quickselect partitions and recurses into one side only, linear on average.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 2. If the pivot lands at k minus one, done
slides.narration: Step by step. First, pick a pivot and partition. Second, if the pivot lands at k minus one, done. Third, else continue on one side.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We partition with the first element as pivot, swapping out-of-place pairs, place the pivot at r, and narrow lo or hi toward the target.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n avg, O of n squared worst. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Worst case O(n²) — randomise the pivot
slides.narration: Worst case is quadratic; randomise the pivot. Remember k is one-indexed.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
slides.narration: Median of medians guarantees linear worst case.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Partition like quicksort, but only recurse into the side containing the kth position.
